In this field, statehood and sovereignty matters because what makes a state and what sovereignty protects. It is taught at the Advanced level of the teaching ladder, building from first principles toward professional practice, with each concept defined before it is used.
overview: International Law is the field concerned with Law between nations: treaties, custom, and the institutions governing a world without a world government. Current Research Frontiers in International Law belongs to its essential core. Concretely: Statehood and sovereignty — what makes a state and what sovereignty protects. And International criminal law — prosecuting genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity. Mastering this entry means being able to explain the topic in plain sentences, recognize it in real cases, and apply it alongside the neighboring ideas of the Advanced tier.
core_concepts: Statehood and sovereignty: what makes a state and what sovereignty protects.
International criminal law: prosecuting genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity.
key_laws: Pacta sunt servanda: treaties must be kept.
Jus cogens: peremptory norms no treaty may violate.
vocabulary: Ratification: a state's formal consent to be bound.
Customary law: binding practice accepted as law.
methods: Treaty interpretation: the Vienna Convention's text-context-purpose method.
history: International law began with Grotius's 1625 treatise; 19th-century conferences codified war and diplomacy. The UN Charter, Geneva Conventions, and human rights treaties rebuilt it after 1945, and international courts now enforce parts of it.
key_points: Statehood and sovereignty: what makes a state and what sovereignty protects.
